title: How an LRU cache decides what to forget
subject: algorithm

brief.audience: programmers who have used a cache but not built one

scenes.why: Opening: the problem every cache has, then the promise to show one answer.

beats.say: A cache has limited room, so when it fills up, something has to go.
beats.text: A full cache has to *forget* something.

beats.say: A least recently used cache makes that choice in the simplest way that works. It drops whatever you touched longest ago.

cues.text:
A full cache has to *forget* something.
LRU drops what you touched *longest ago*.

scenes.why: The two fields only mean something once you see them: a size limit, and a row that keeps its order.
scenes.heading: lru_cache.py · what it stores

beats.say: The whole cache is one small class with two pieces of state.
A capacity, which is how many entries it may hold.
And an ordered dictionary, which remembers the order its keys were last touched. Oldest at the front, newest at the back.

scenes.why: One line of get() reorders the row; showing the line and the jump together makes the link.
scenes.heading: lru_cache.py · get

beats.say: Reading a key counts as a use. Say we ask for A.
A is cached, so move_to_end sends it to the newest end, and the others shift down.

scenes.why: put() is two decisions; each one is a line of code and a visible effect on the same row.
scenes.heading: lru_cache.py · put

beats.say: Writing has two decisions in it. First, is this key already cached?
B is, so it is refreshed, exactly like a read, and the new value is stored.
Second decision. Did that push us over capacity? Three entries, capacity three, so nothing is evicted.
But write a key the cache has never seen, and the row grows to four.
Now the check fails, so popitem drops the oldest end, and we are back within our limit.

scenes.why: Recap: three claims the viewer should leave with.
scenes.title: What to remember

items.text: Order of use lives in one ordered dictionary
Every read and write moves a key to the newest end
Over capacity? Drop the oldest end
That is how it decides what to forget

beats.say: So, three things to remember. The order of use lives in a single ordered dictionary.
Every read and every write moves a key to the newest end.
And when the cache is over capacity, it drops the oldest end. That is how it decides what to forget.
